items.question: Two devices, A and B, together cost $720. The price of device A is then raised by 25% and the price of device B is reduced by 20%. After the two changes, the two devices together cost $792. What was the original price of device A?
items.explanation: Let the original price of A be a dollars, so B originally cost 720 minus a dollars. After the changes, 1.25a plus 0.8(720 minus a) equals 792, so 0.45a plus 576 equals 792 and a equals 480. The $240 option is the original price of B, $360 is half the original total, $396 is half the new total, and $600 is the price of A after its rise.

items.question: An integer n lies between 60 and 160. When n is divided by 7 the remainder is 3, when n is divided by 4 the remainder is 1, and n is divisible by 3. What is the value of n?
items.explanation: The first two conditions together leave n in a single arithmetic progression, and only one value in that progression inside the range is also divisible by 3: 129. Each other option satisfies at most two of the three conditions, so a solver who uses only one or two of them cannot pin n down.

items.question: A shopkeeper buys one item for $600 and sells it at a profit of 40%, and buys a second item for $400. At what loss percentage must the second item be sold for the shopkeeper to break even overall, taking both items together?
options: 30% loss
40% loss
60% loss
50% loss
25% loss
items.explanation: The profit on the first item is $600 x 40% = $240. To break even overall the second item must lose exactly that $240, which on a cost of $400 is $240 / $400 = 60% loss. Averaging the two percentages, or using the first item's profit percentage for the second item, gives the distractors.

items.question: A sum is invested for two years. In the first year it earns simple interest at 5% per annum, and in the second year the rate rises to 10% per annum. If the interest had instead been compounded annually at the same two rates, the total interest would have been $50 more than the simple interest. What total interest would the same sum have earned if it had instead been invested at compound interest of 8% per annum for two years?
items.explanation: The compounding difference equals principal x 5 x 10 / 10000, so the principal is $50 x 10000 / (5 x 10) = $10,000. At 8% compound for two years the interest is $10,000 x (1.08 squared minus 1) = $1,664. Simple interest at the new rate, the interest under the original compounding ($1500 simple plus $50 difference), and one year of interest give the distractors.

items.question: Class A has 18 students with an average score of 70, and class B has 25 students with an average score of 55. Scores range from 0 to 100. 2 students are moved from class B to class A, chosen so that class A's new average is as high as possible. What is class A's new average?
items.explanation: To maximise class A's average, the moved students must be class B's highest scorers, who can score at most 100 each. Class A's total becomes 18 x 70 + 2 x 100 = 1460, over 20 students, giving 1460 / 20 = 73. The correct option is 73. Moving average or low scorers, or assuming the maximum score itself is the answer, gives the distractors.

items.question: A car travels 150 km at 50 km/h, then 100 km at 40 km/h. Before the third leg the driver stops for a one-hour break. The car then travels a further 200 km. Counting the break as part of the journey time, the average speed for the whole 450 km journey must be 60 km/h. At what speed must the car travel on the third leg?
options: 100 km/h
200 km/h
60 km/h
112 km/h
items.explanation: The first two legs take 3 hours and 2.5 hours. For an overall average of 60 km/h over 450 km, the whole journey including the break must take 7.5 hours, leaving 1 hours for the third leg after the one-hour break. The required speed is 200 / 1 = 200 km/h. Ignoring the break, or averaging the speeds, gives the distractors.

items.question: Worker A can finish a job in 20 days and worker B can finish the same job in 30 days. They start working together, but after 5 days A leaves and B finishes the job alone, working at half speed because B must now handle the loading as well as the work. How many days in total does the job take?
options: 22.5 days
30 days
40 days
12 days
20 days
items.explanation: Together they complete 1/20 + 1/30 of the job per day, so in 5 days they complete 5/12 of it, leaving 7/12. B alone at half speed completes 1/60 of the job per day, so the remaining 7/12 takes 35 more days, for a total of 5 + 35 = 40 days. Using B's full speed after A leaves, or the original together-time alone, gives the distractors.

items.question: Group A has 20 students with an average score of 95, and group B has 30 students with an average score of 75. A third group, group C, has an average score of 90. When all three groups are combined, the average score is 85. How many students are in group C?
items.explanation: Groups A and B together total 4150 points over 50 students. If group C has n students, the combined average is (4150 + 90n) / (50 + n) = 85, which gives n = 20. Using only the two-group ratio, or the combined average of A and B alone, gives the distractors.

items.question: Which of the following is the largest, and which is the second largest: 2^48, 3^36, 5^24, 11^12? Give the largest first, then the second largest.
items.explanation: Rewrite each with the common exponent 12: 2^48 = (16)^12, 3^36 = (27)^12, 5^24 = (25)^12, 11^12 = (11)^12. Ordering the bases gives 3^36 largest and 5^24 second largest. Comparing the bases or the exponents alone, or swapping the two places, gives the distractors.

items.question: x and y are positive integers with x greater than y. x squared plus y squared is 169, and x minus y is 7. What is the value of x?
items.explanation: The sum x plus y must be found first. (x plus y) squared equals 2(x squared plus y squared) minus (x minus y) squared, which is 2 times 169 minus 49, or 289, so x plus y is 17. With x minus y equal to 7, adding the two equations gives 2x equals 24, so x is 12. The 5 option is y, 17 is x plus y, 7 is the difference, and 14 satisfies neither equation.

items.question: A bag contains 5 red balls and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. Given that at least one of the two balls drawn is red, what is the probability that the second ball drawn is red?
items.explanation: The condition changes the sample space, so the unconditional probability 5/7 is not the answer. The probability that the second ball is red is 5/7. The probability that at least one ball is red is 1 minus (2/7 times 1/6), which is 20/21. The conditional probability is therefore (5/7) divided by (20/21), which is 3/4. Counting ordered pairs gives the same result: 40 of the 42 ordered pairs contain at least one red ball, and 30 of those have a red second ball.

items.question: How many pairs (a, b) of integers with 1 at most a, a less than b, and b at most 30 satisfy the following: a plus b divides a squared plus b squared?
items.explanation: Since a squared plus b squared equals the square of a plus b minus 2ab, the condition that a plus b divides a squared plus b squared holds exactly when a plus b divides 2ab. Let d be the greatest common divisor of a and b, and write a as d times x and b as d times y, where x and y are coprime positive integers with x less than y. Then a plus b equals d times the quantity x plus y, and 2ab equals 2 times d squared times x times y, so the condition becomes that x plus y divides 2 times d times x times y. Now x plus y is coprime to x and coprime to y, since any common divisor of x plus y and x also divides y, and x and y are coprime, so x plus y is coprime to the product x times y. Hence x plus y must divide 2d. This is where the parity of x and y matters: if x plus y is odd, then x plus y divides d; if x plus y is even, which happens exactly when x and y are both odd, then only half of x plus y need divide d. So for each coprime pair (x, y), the admissible values of d are the multiples of x plus y when x plus y is odd, and the multiples of half of x plus y when x plus y is even, with d times y at most 30. Counting by s equal to x plus y: for s equal to 3, the pair (1, 2) gives d equal to 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15, which is 5 pairs; for s equal to 4, the pair (1, 3) gives d equal to 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, which is 5 pairs; for s equal to 5, the pair (1, 4) gives d equal to 5 only, and the pair (2, 3) gives d equal to 5 and 10, which is 3 pairs; for s equal to 6, the pair (1, 5) gives d equal to 3 and 6, which is 2 pairs; for s equal to 7, the pairs (1, 6) and (2, 5) give nothing, since d equal to 7 already makes d times y exceed 30, and the pair (3, 4) gives d equal to 7, which is 1 pair; for s equal to 8, the pairs (1, 7) and (3, 5) give d equal to 4 each, which is 2 pairs. For s at least 9 there is nothing: if s is odd, d times y is at least s times the quantity s plus 1 over 2, which is at least 45; if s is even and at least 12, d times y is at least s times the quantity s plus 2 over 4, which is at least 42; and for s equal to 10 the only coprime pairs are (1, 9) and (3, 7), with d times y at least 45 and 35. The total is 5 plus 5 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 plus 2, which is 18. Requiring x plus y to divide d in all cases, which ignores the even case, gives 12; raising the bound to 36 gives 22; counting ordered pairs doubles the counts to 24 and 36.

items.question: How many integers x satisfy both of the following conditions: the absolute value of (x - 1) is less than 7, and x squared is less than 40?
items.explanation: The first condition gives -6 < x < 8, and the second gives -6 <= x <= 6 in integers, since 6 squared is 36 and 7 squared is 49. Intersecting them leaves the integers -5 to 6, which is 12 integers. The correct option is 12. Counting from one condition alone, or including the endpoints, gives the distractors.

items.question: If f(x) = x squared -2x -3, how many integers x from 0 to 5 inclusive satisfy f(x + 1) < 0?
items.explanation: Substituting gives f(x + 1) = (x + 1) squared -2(x + 1) -3, which simplifies to x squared - 4, or (x + 2)(x - 2). This is negative exactly when -2 < x < 2, so among the integers from 0 to 5 only x = 0, 1 qualify, which is 2 integers. The correct option is 2. Forgetting the shift, or including the boundary where the expression is zero, gives the distractors.

items.question: A sequence is defined by a(1) = 1 and a(n+1) = a(n) + 2n for n >= 1. What is the smallest value of n for which a(n) is greater than 750?
items.explanation: Adding the steps gives a closed form: a(n) = 1 + 2 x (1 + 2 + ... + (n - 1)) = 1 + n(n - 1). At n = 27, a(n) = 703, which does not exceed 750; at n = 28, a(n) = 757, which does. So the smallest such n is 28. Stopping at the first n whose step alone exceeds the threshold, or summing the wrong range of indices, gives the distractors.

items.question: In a survey of 150 people, 80 use product A, 70 use product B, and 50 use product C. 30 use both A and B, 20 use both A and C, and 18 use both B and C. 8 use all three products. How many people use exactly one of the three products?
items.explanation: Only A: 80 - 30 - 20 + 8 = 38. Only B: 70 - 30 - 18 + 8 = 30. Only C: 50 - 20 - 18 + 8 = 20. Adding them gives 38 + 30 + 20 = 88. The number using at least one product (140), the old two-product answer, and the raw counts give the distractors.

items.question: How many arrangements of the six letters A, B, C, D, E and F are there in a row such that E is between A and B, with A occurring before E and E occurring before B, C is not next to D, and F is not at either end of the row?
items.explanation: Place A, E and B first, in that order. Choose three positions out of six for them in increasing order, which can be done in 20 ways, with A first, E in the middle and B last. The remaining three slots go to C, D and F. For a given choice of the three positions, F must take a slot that is not an end, and the two slots left for C and D must not be adjacent. In 12 of the 20 placements exactly one choice for F leaves C and D non-adjacent, and in the other 8 placements exactly two choices do, because which slots remain for C and D depends on where A, E and B sit. C and D can then be placed in 2 orders, giving 12 times 1 times 2 plus 8 times 2 times 2, which is 24 plus 32, or 56 arrangements. The 80 counts arrangements satisfying only E between A and B in this order and one of the other two restrictions, 120 counts E between A and B in this order alone, 240 counts A before B with C not next to D, ignoring the E-between and F restrictions, and 336 counts C not next to D with F not at an end, ignoring E between A and B.

items.question: Class B has 30 students with an average score of 60, and scores range from 0 to 100. 5 students are moved from class B to another class, chosen so that the receiving class's average is as high as possible. What is the highest possible average score of the students left in class B?
items.explanation: Maximising the receiving class means moving class B's highest scorers, who score 100 each. Class B's total falls from 30 x 60 = 1800 to 1300, over 25 students, giving 1300 / 25 = 52. The correct option is 52. Moving the lowest scorers would raise class B's average instead, and moving average scorers would leave it unchanged, which are the traps here.

items.question:
Let x = 3^n + 7^n, where n is a positive integer. Which of the following could be the units digit of x?

I. 8
II. 0
III. 4
options: II only
III only
I and II only
None
I only
items.explanation: The units digits of 3^n cycle through [3, 9, 7, 1], and those of 7^n through [7, 9, 3, 1]. Adding the cycles, the possible units digits of x are [0, 2, 8]. So 8, 0 can occur and the other value cannot. The correct option is I and II only. Testing only n = 1 misses the later cycle values, which is the trap here.

items.question: A sum of money is divided between two partners. The first partner invests his share in a scheme that grows by 10%, while the second partner keeps his share as cash. After the period, the two partners hold equal amounts, and together they hold $2,200. What was the original sum?
items.explanation: Let the first partner's share be a fraction f of the original sum S. Equality of the final amounts gives f x (1 + 0.1) = 1 - f, so f = 0.48. The total held is 2 x (1 - f) x S = $2,200, so S = $2,100. The correct option is $2,100. Answering with the final total, or with half of it, ignores that only one share grew, which is the trap here.

items.question: Eight distinct integers have a mean of 15, a median of 14 and a range of 20. What is the least possible value of the second smallest of the eight integers?
items.explanation: Write the integers a1 to a8 in increasing order. The sum is 120, the median gives a4 plus a5 equals 28, and the range gives a8 equals a1 plus 20. Suppose a2 is at most 5. Then a1 is at most 4, so a8 is at most 24 and a6 plus a7 plus a8 is at most 22 plus 23 plus 24, or 69. Also a4 is at most 13, since a4 is less than a5 and the two sum to 28, so a3 is at most 12. The total is then at most (4 plus 5) plus 12 plus 28 plus 69, which is 118, less than 120, a contradiction. So a2 is at least 6, and 6 is achieved by (5, 6, 9, 13, 15, 23, 24, 25), which sums to 120, has median 14 and range 20. The least possible second smallest value is 6.

items.question: FreshChoice Grocers plans to increase sales of bottled juices by 18% by placing them at eye level in every store. The plan assumes that shelf position is the main factor limiting sales of these products. The stores were not chosen at random: managers volunteered their stores for the redesign. The chain also ran local advertising for bottled juices in 10 of the 16 redesigned stores. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the plan?
options: Stores that received both eye-level placement and local advertising showed the largest rise in sales of bottled juices.
Several rival stores also stock bottled juices at eye level.
The stores that volunteered for the redesign were already growing faster than other stores before the change.
Customers said they liked the new eye-level displays and found the products easier to see.

Stores that received eye-level placement but no local advertising, and were chosen by head office rather than volunteering, showed no rise in sales of bottled juices, while stores that ran local advertising did rise.
items.explanation: The plan is threatened only by evidence that separates the two changes from the selection effect. The key option does exactly that: placement without advertising, in stores that did not volunteer, produced no rise, while advertising did, so the rise points to advertising, not position. The both-changes option is confounded, since both changes happened together. The volunteering fact alone shows selection but does not separate advertising from placement. Customers liking the displays is an attitude, not a sales effect, and rival behaviour is irrelevant.

items.question: In Brookfield, traffic accidents fell by 35% after the city installed speed cameras on major roads. Traffic volume on those roads was unchanged over the period. Two other things happened at the same time. First, the city posted lower speed limits on the camera roads. Second, the camera roads were chosen because accidents on them had spiked to about double their long-run average in the year before the cameras were installed, while other major roads had not spiked. The city council concluded that the cameras caused the fall. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the council's conclusion?
options: During the same period, the city also closed several accident-prone roads for long-term repairs, but those roads had carried only 3% of the city's traffic and 2% of its accidents before they closed.
On roads elsewhere that received lower speed limits but no cameras, accidents fell by 9%.
Some drivers now avoid the roads with cameras, driving instead on minor roads.
Average journey times on the camera roads rose slightly after the cameras were installed.

Major roads in Brookfield that received neither cameras nor lower speed limits, but had also seen accidents spike to about double their long-run average the year before, saw accidents fall by 33% over the same period.
items.explanation: The key option shows almost the whole fall happening with neither intervention: roads with the same pre-installation spike, but no cameras and no lower limits, fell by 33%, against the 35% fall on the camera roads. That points to the fall being a return toward the long-run average after a spike, not an effect of the cameras or the limits. The closures touched only 2% of accidents, far too little to explain a 35% fall. Lower limits alone explain only 9%, leaving most of the fall unexplained, so it weakens the conclusion only partly. Driver avoidance does not reduce accidents across the city, and slower journeys are consistent with the cameras working.

items.question: A supermarket chain rearranged the layout of 40 stores and reported that total sales rose by 6 percent in the following quarter. The chain concluded that the new layout caused the rise. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the chain's conclusion?
options: Sales rose most in the departments whose layout was changed.

Sales were flat in the departments whose layout was changed, sales rose only in the departments the layout did not touch, and the rise began in the week a large competitor near those stores closed down.
Sales rose by 1 percent at a rival chain that changed nothing.
Customers said they liked the new layout.
The new layout cost the chain more than expected.
items.explanation: Step 1, the wrong place: if the layout caused the rise, the rise should appear where the layout changed, but sales there were flat, so the layout explains nothing. Step 2, the wrong categories: the rise is concentrated exactly in the departments the layout did not touch, where it cannot have caused it. Step 3, the timing and the alternative: the rise began in the week a large competitor closed down, which explains why customers spent more at these stores. The three facts together leave the layout with no part of the rise to explain. The first option would strengthen the conclusion; the third option explains only 1 of the 6 points; customers' opinions say nothing about what caused sales to rise; the cost of the layout is irrelevant.

items.question: Summit Lending found that customers who use its budgeting app save more than customers who do not. The bank concluded that the app itself helps customers save. The bank also ran branch workshops on saving for some customers at the same time. Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the bank's conclusion?
options: Customers who save more tend to use more banking products.

Customers who were randomly assigned the app, and received no other new service, saved more than a matched control group, while a separate group that attended only the branch workshops saved no more than the control group.
The bank advertises the app heavily.
The app was launched two years ago.
Customers who were randomly assigned the app saved more than a matched control group that was not given the app.
items.explanation: The conclusion has to survive two gaps at once: the app may simply attract people who already save, and the branch workshops may be doing the work instead. The key option closes both: random assignment removes the selection gap, and the separate group shows the workshops alone produced no extra saving, while the app group, with no other new service, did save more. Random assignment alone leaves the workshop gap open. Popularity, advertising, product use and the launch date do not connect the app to saving.

items.question: A gym chain introduced a new class timetable at its branches and reported that membership renewals rose from 60 percent to 72 percent in the following year. The chain concluded that the new timetable caused the rise. In the same year, a rival gym chain with branches in the same towns closed down. Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the chain's conclusion?
options: Members who attended the new classes said they enjoyed them.
In the six months after the rival chain closed, renewals at the gym's branches rose to 74 percent.

Renewals rose by the same 12 points at branches in towns where the rival chain stayed open as at branches in towns where it closed, and renewals at a sister chain that kept the old timetable were flat in both kinds of town.
Renewals rose from 60 percent to 63 percent in the six months before the rival chain closed.
The new timetable cost the chain less than expected.
items.explanation: Step 1, falsify the rival: if the rival's closure caused the rise, the rise should appear only in towns where the rival closed, but renewals rose by the same 12 points in towns where the rival stayed open, so the closure cannot explain the rise. Step 2, rule out a general trend: the sister chain, which kept the old timetable, was flat in both kinds of town, so the rise is not a town-wide trend either. Step 3, the two comparisons together leave the timetable as the explanation that fits both patterns. The second option is measured after the closure, exactly what the rival explanation predicts; the fourth option leaves 9 of the 12 points unexplained; members' opinions and the cost say nothing about renewals.

items.question: CloudNine Air will add a late-night flight because surveys show that business travellers want later departures. No rival airline currently offers a late-night flight on the route. The airline expects the new flight to be profitable. Which of the following is an assumption on which the airline's expectation depends?
options: The airline has aircraft available for a late-night departure.
Business travellers prefer late-night flights to early-morning ones.
Surveys are a reliable way to measure traveller preferences.
Other airlines do not offer late-night flights on the route.
Enough business travellers will actually book the late-night flight at fares that cover its cost, and no rival will add a competing late-night flight before the new flight launches.
items.explanation: Wanting a later departure does not guarantee booking at a profitable fare, and the absence of a rival today helps only if no rival enters before launch and splits the demand, so the profit expectation depends on both. The other options are either stated in the argument, irrelevant to profitability, or background: aircraft availability does not ensure demand, survey reliability is not the link between desire and purchase, and a preference for late over early flights does not show travellers will pay covering fares.

items.question: A clinic will cut patient waiting times by hiring more doctors, since a shortage of doctors is the bottleneck in its process. Which of the following is an assumption on which the clinic's plan depends?
options: Patients arrive evenly through the day.

The extra doctors will actually be able to see more patients, with consultation rooms and support staff available for them, and no other stage, such as triage or test results, will become the new bottleneck once more doctors are in place.
Waiting times are currently the clinic's main complaint.
The clinic can afford the extra salaries.
Doctors are willing to work at the clinic.
items.explanation: Hiring doctors cuts waiting times only if the extra doctors can actually see more patients, which needs rooms and support staff, and only if no other stage becomes the new bottleneck, so the plan depends on both. Even arrivals, current complaints, affordability and willingness to work do not guarantee that patients move through the clinic faster.

items.question: At NetWise Solutions, 250 engineers completed the advanced training and 250 did not. 50% of engineers who completed the advanced training were promoted within a year, while only 20% of engineers who did not complete it were promoted. The training is voluntary and takes six months. Which of the following must be true?
options: Most engineers at the company completed the training.
The advanced training causes promotions.
Engineers who do not complete the training cannot be promoted.
More than three-quarters of the engineers promoted within a year had completed the training.
More than a third of all engineers at the company were promoted within a year.
items.explanation: Promoted completers number 250 x 50% = 125, and promoted non-completers number 250 x 20% = 50, so 175 of the 500 engineers were promoted, which is 35% of the company, more than a third. The training is voluntary, so causation cannot be inferred; 50 non-completers were promoted, so promotion without training is possible; completers are 250 of 500, not a majority; and completers are 125 of the 175 promoted, under three-quarters.

items.question: In Cedar Falls, a new public library opened and book borrowing rose sharply, yet sales at the city's bookshops also rose in the same year, even though the library lends books for free. The library ran gardening workshops. Sales of gardening books rose sharply, while other categories were flat. Two explanations are offered: (i) the workshops created new gardeners who bought gardening books; (ii) the city's population grew by 20 percent. Which of the following best assesses the two explanations?
options: (i) alone explains the pattern, because it accounts for the rise in gardening books and the flatness of other categories, while (ii) would raise all categories, not gardening books alone.
(ii) alone explains the pattern, because a larger population buys more books of every kind.
Both explanations explain the pattern equally well.
Neither explains the pattern, because libraries and bookshops serve different readers.
(i) explains the rise in borrowing but not the rise in sales.
items.explanation: The pattern has two parts: gardening books rose sharply and other categories were flat. Explanation (i) accounts for both, since new gardeners buy gardening books specifically. Explanation (ii) predicts a rise across all categories, which contradicts the flatness of the others, so it cannot explain the pattern. Option B ignores the flat categories. Option C treats an explanation that fits with one that does not. Option D ignores the workshop link. Option E misstates what (i) explains, since new gardeners buying books is exactly a rise in sales.

items.question: A regional bank is considering closing its rural branches. **Rural branches serve fewer customers per branch than urban branches.** **Closing the rural branches would therefore save the bank money.** Yet the bank's own survey found that **most rural customers would close their accounts entirely if their local branch shut, and the deposits those customers hold are large.** Those deposits are worth far more to the bank than the operating costs the closures would save. The bank should keep its rural branches open. In the argument, the boldfaced statements play which of the following roles?
options: The first is evidence offered in support of the main conclusion; the second is the main conclusion; the third is an assumption the argument depends on.
The first is evidence offered in support of the second statement; the second is a conclusion the argument goes on to reject; the third is evidence offered against the second statement.
The first is a consideration that counts against the main conclusion; the second is the main conclusion; the third is evidence offered in support of it.
The first is the main conclusion; the second is evidence offered in support of it; the third is an intermediate conclusion.
The first is an assumption the argument depends on; the second is an intermediate conclusion that supports the main conclusion; the third is the main conclusion.
items.explanation: The first statement is a fact offered to support the claim that closing the branches would save money, which is why the second statement follows it with therefore. But the second statement is not the argument's conclusion: the survey evidence and the final sentence overturn it, since the deposits at stake exceed any saving in operating costs, so the second statement is a provisional conclusion the argument rejects. The third statement is the survey finding itself, evidence that counts against the second statement and in support of the real main conclusion, which is the unboldfaced final sentence that the bank should keep its rural branches open. Option A fails because the second statement is not the main conclusion and the third is stated evidence, not an assumption. Option C fails because the second statement is rejected, not defended. Option D reverses the roles of the first two statements. Option E fails because the first statement is a stated fact, not an assumption, and the third statement is evidence, not the main conclusion.

items.passage: For forty years, manufacturers worshipped leanness. Just-in-time production, pioneered by Toyota, kept inventories near zero, with parts arriving hours before they were needed. The system was elegant: less capital tied up in warehouses, less waste, faster detection of defects. It also worked beautifully until it did not. A single disruption, a pandemic, a blocked canal, an earthquake, could idle factories on the other side of the world, because there was no buffer to absorb the shock. The pandemic exposed the fragility at scale. Car makers could not finish vehicles for want of a single chip; hospitals ran short of basic supplies. The response has not been a wholesale return to stockpiling, which would surrender the efficiency gains. The firms described here are large manufacturers of cars and electronics. Small suppliers and service businesses, which hold little stock in any case, were not surveyed, and the passage makes no claim about how they responded. Instead, firms are adopting a middle course: just-in-case buffers for critical components, dual sourcing from different regions, and real-time visibility into suppliers several tiers deep. The shift reveals a deeper point about efficiency. A system optimised for a stable world is fragile in an unstable one, and the cost of that fragility only becomes visible when the shock arrives. The new goal is not maximum leanness but resilience, the ability to keep operating when the next disruption comes, even at the price of carrying a little more stock.
items.question: Which of the following best states the passage's main argument, with the evidence for it correctly limited?
options: Just-in-time manufacturing is efficient but fragile, and firms are now balancing leanness with resilience. The evidence discussed comes from large manufacturers of cars and electronics.

Just-in-time manufacturing is efficient but fragile, and firms are now balancing leanness with resilience. The evidence discussed covers every kind of business, including small suppliers and service businesses.
Stockpiling is the best strategy. The evidence discussed comes from large manufacturers of cars and electronics.
Just-in-time manufacturing always fails. The evidence discussed covers every kind of business, including small suppliers and service businesses.
Supply chains are unimportant. The evidence discussed comes from large manufacturers of cars and electronics.
items.explanation: Only the first option gets both parts right: the thesis is the passage's main argument, and the evidence behind it is limited to large manufacturers of cars and electronics. The second option keeps the thesis but extends the evidence to every kind of business, including small suppliers and service businesses, which the passage never covers. The other options state a thesis the passage rejects or never makes, so getting the scope right cannot save them.

items.question: Which of the following pairs two claims that the passage actually supports?
options: (i) The firms described are large manufacturers of cars and electronics, not small suppliers or service businesses. (ii) The findings apply to every firm in every industry.

(i) The firms described include small suppliers and service businesses as well. (ii) The case for resilience over maximum leanness rests on large manufacturers, so it does not establish how small suppliers or service businesses should respond.
(i) The firms described include small suppliers and service businesses as well. (ii) The findings apply to every firm in every industry.
(i) The firms described are large manufacturers of cars and electronics, not small suppliers or service businesses. (ii) The passage proves leanness always fails.

(i) The firms described are large manufacturers of cars and electronics, not small suppliers or service businesses. (ii) The case for resilience over maximum leanness rests on large manufacturers, so it does not establish how small suppliers or service businesses should respond.
items.explanation: Both parts must be true. The first part of the key states the passage's own limit on its evidence, and the second part states the qualified conclusion the passage actually draws. Each distractor pairs a true part with a false one: an overclaim that extends the evidence beyond its limit, a scope the passage explicitly excludes, or a claim the passage contradicts.

items.question: The passage's account of firms adopting buffers, dual sourcing and real-time visibility applies most directly to which firms?
options: Small suppliers that hold little stock in any case.
Service businesses.
Hospitals that ran short of basic supplies.
Large manufacturers of cars and electronics, since small suppliers and service businesses were not surveyed and the passage makes no claim about how they responded.
All manufacturers everywhere, whatever their size.
items.explanation: The passage states that the firms described are large manufacturers of cars and electronics, and that small suppliers and service businesses, which hold little stock in any case, were not surveyed, with the passage making no claim about how they responded. So the account applies most directly to large car and electronics manufacturers. Hospitals appear only as an example of shortages, not as firms adopting the middle course, and extending the account to small suppliers, service businesses or all manufacturers ignores the passage's own limit.

items.question: Which of the following best captures the author's view of efficiency?
options: The author believes maximum leanness is always best.
The author believes firms should return to wholesale stockpiling.

The author believes a system optimised for a stable world is fragile in an unstable one, and favours resilience even at the price of carrying a little more stock, but the account concerns large manufacturers of cars and electronics, not small suppliers or service businesses.
The author believes efficiency does not matter at all.
The author believes just-in-time production never worked.
items.explanation: The passage says a system optimised for a stable world is fragile in an unstable one, that the cost of that fragility only becomes visible when the shock arrives, and that the new goal is resilience even at the price of carrying a little more stock, not a return to stockpiling. It also states that the firms described are large manufacturers of cars and electronics, with small suppliers and service businesses not surveyed. The author never says leanness always wins, never says efficiency is irrelevant, and acknowledges that just-in-time worked beautifully until it did not.

items.question: Which of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
options: Disruption can never be absorbed by any firm.
The case for resilience over maximum leanness rests on large manufacturers, so it does not establish how small suppliers or service businesses should respond.
The passage proves every firm must carry buffer stock.
Service businesses face the same fragility as car makers.
The author concludes leanness is always best.
items.explanation: The passage argues the new goal is resilience, but its evidence is large manufacturers, so the strongest supported claim is qualified to them. The distractors demand buffer stock of everyone, extend fragility to unstudied businesses, reverse the argument against maximum leanness, or state an absolute the passage contradicts.

items.passage: Every two weeks, somewhere in the world, the last fluent speaker of a language dies, and with them goes a library: oral histories, medicinal knowledge, poetry, and ways of seeing the world that have no exact translation. Linguists estimate that of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, nearly half are endangered, and most will fall silent within a century. The causes are familiar: schooling in a dominant language, migration to cities, and the economic advantage of speaking the language of jobs and media. Parents stop passing a language to children not out of indifference but because they want their children to succeed, and a language not learned by children is a language dying. Yet the story is not only one of loss. Hebrew was revived from a liturgical language into a living mother tongue. Maori and Hawaiian, once banned in schools, are now taught to children through immersion programmes, and their speaker numbers are rising. Revival is possible, but it is hard. The revivals described, Hebrew, Maori and Hawaiian, all had state support and schooling behind them. Languages revived by small communities without such support are not discussed, and the passage does not claim they would follow the same path. It requires more than dictionaries and recordings; it requires a community of speakers using the language daily, in homes, schools and workplaces. Technology helps at the margins: apps and online archives let scattered speakers practise together, but no app can replace a neighbourhood where children hear the language every day. A language survives when it is lived, not merely documented.
items.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the author's view of technology in language revival?
options: The author believes every endangered language can be revived.
The author believes technology is useless.
Technology helps at the margins, but revival needs a community using the language daily, and the revivals cited all had state support behind them.
The author believes apps alone can save a language.
Small communities without state support revived their languages the same way.
items.explanation: The passage says technology helps at the margins but no app replaces a neighbourhood where children hear the language daily, and limits its revivals to state-supported cases. The distractors credit apps alone, extend the examples to unstudied communities, promise universal revival, or deny technology any role.

items.question: Which of the following pairs two claims that the passage actually supports?
options: (i) Hebrew, Maori and Hawaiian all had state support and schooling behind them. (ii) Every endangered language has been revived this way.
(i) Hebrew, Maori and Hawaiian all had state support and schooling behind them. (ii) language revival is possible under the right conditions.
(i) The revivals were driven by small communities without state support. (ii) language revival is possible under the right conditions.
(i) The revivals were driven by small communities without state support. (ii) Every endangered language has been revived this way.
(i) Hebrew, Maori and Hawaiian all had state support and schooling behind them. (ii) The passage argues revival is impossible.
items.explanation: Both parts must be true. The first part of the key states the passage's own limit on its evidence, and the second part states the qualified conclusion the passage actually draws. Each distractor pairs a true part with a false one: an overclaim that extends the evidence beyond its limit, a scope the passage explicitly excludes, or a claim the passage contradicts.

items.question: The mention of Hebrew, Maori and Hawaiian, together with the passage's limit, most strongly suggests that
options: revival is easy for any endangered language.
technology alone can revive a language.
revival is possible but hard, and these revivals all had state support and schooling behind them, so the passage does not claim small communities without such support would follow the same path.
all endangered languages will revive.
state support is unnecessary for revival.
items.explanation: The three revivals are presented as proof that revival is possible, immediately followed by the warning that it is hard, and the passage states that the revivals described all had state support and schooling behind them, that languages revived by small communities without such support are not discussed, and that it does not claim they would follow the same path. So the mention supports possible but hard revival under state support, not easy revival, not technology alone, and not revival without support.

items.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following?
options: Small communities without state support have revived their languages just as Hebrew, Maori and Hawaiian did.
Technology is useless in language revival.
A language can survive if it is documented in dictionaries and recordings, even if no community speaks it daily.
Revival requires a community using the language daily, and the cited revivals all had state support, so a revival without such support cannot be assumed to follow the same path.
Every endangered language can be revived with enough apps.
items.explanation: The passage says revival requires a community of speakers using the language daily, and that the revivals described, Hebrew, Maori and Hawaiian, all had state support and schooling behind them. It expressly says languages revived by small communities without such support are not discussed and the passage does not claim they would follow the same path. The fourth option combines both points. The first contradicts the scope limit, the second contradicts the passage's statement that technology helps at the margins, the third contradicts the claim that a language survives when it is lived, and the fifth contradicts the passage's insistence that revival is hard.

items.passage: Photosynthesis is the most important chemical reaction on Earth, and also one of the least efficient. Plants convert only one or two percent of the sunlight they absorb into biomass, and the rest is lost as heat or reflected away. For most of agricultural history, that inefficiency did not matter much: yields rose through better seeds, fertiliser and irrigation, not through faster photosynthesis. But those gains are slowing, and the world's population keeps growing. Some scientists now argue that the next great yield increase must come from the process itself. The most promising target is photorespiration, a wasteful side reaction in which the enzyme that captures carbon dioxide sometimes grabs oxygen instead, undoing part of the plant's work. In some crops, photorespiration wastes up to a quarter of the energy the plant captures. Researchers have engineered tobacco plants with a shortcut that bypasses photorespiration, and those plants grew up to forty percent larger in field trials. Those field trials were run in the American Midwest under controlled irrigation. Trials in tropical smallholder conditions, where water and soil vary widely, have not yet been reported, and the passage draws no conclusion about them. Rice and wheat, the crops that feed billions, are harder: their biology is more complex, and the shortcut must work without unintended side effects. Critics warn that field trials in one place may not transfer to the varied conditions where food is actually grown, and that focusing on a single process risks neglecting soil, water and pests. The debate is not whether photosynthesis can be improved, but whether the improvement will survive the journey from laboratory to farm.
items.question: Which of the following can be inferred about the author's view of improving photosynthesis?
options: Improving photosynthesis is the most promising next step, but the trial evidence comes from the American Midwest, so it does not show the improvement will work in tropical smallholder conditions.
The shortcut will raise yields everywhere.
Tropical smallholder trials have already succeeded.
The author believes photosynthesis cannot be improved.
The author believes soil, water and pests do not matter.
items.explanation: The passage calls the process the most promising target, then limits the trials to the controlled Midwest and notes critics who warn about transfer. The distractors promise universal yields, claim unreported trials, reverse the passage's optimism, or dismiss the critics' concerns the passage takes seriously.

items.question: Which of the following pairs two claims that the passage actually supports?
options: (i) They were run in the American Midwest under controlled irrigation. (ii) note that trial results may not transfer to varied farming conditions, as part of a debate about whether the improvement will survive the journey from laboratory to farm.
(i) They were run in the American Midwest under controlled irrigation. (ii) They covered every farming region.

(i) They were run in tropical smallholder conditions. (ii) note that trial results may not transfer to varied farming conditions, as part of a debate about whether the improvement will survive the journey from laboratory to farm.
(i) They were run in tropical smallholder conditions. (ii) They covered every farming region.
(i) They were run in the American Midwest under controlled irrigation. (ii) They prove rice and wheat will grow forty percent larger.
items.explanation: Both parts must be true. The first part of the key states the passage's own limit on its evidence, and the second part states the qualified conclusion the passage actually draws. Each distractor pairs a true part with a false one: an overclaim that extends the evidence beyond its limit, a scope the passage explicitly excludes, or a claim the passage contradicts.

items.question: Critics of the photosynthesis work warn that field trials in one place may not transfer to the varied conditions where food is actually grown. Given the passage's qualifications, what follows?
options: Photosynthesis cannot be improved.
Rice and wheat already use the shortcut.

The tobacco shortcut grew larger plants in American Midwest trials under controlled irrigation, but trials in tropical smallholder conditions have not been reported, so the improvement may not survive the journey from laboratory to farm.
Critics oppose all research into higher yields.
Midwest trials prove the shortcut will work in tropical smallholder conditions.
items.explanation: The passage says researchers engineered tobacco plants with a shortcut that bypasses photorespiration, and those plants grew up to forty percent larger in field trials, but those trials were run in the American Midwest under controlled irrigation, and trials in tropical smallholder conditions have not yet been reported. The debate is not whether photosynthesis can be improved, but whether the improvement will survive the journey from laboratory to farm. So the Midwest result does not prove tropical success, rice and wheat do not already use the shortcut, and the critics are not opposing all yield research.

items.question: Which of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
options: Smallholder trials confirm the results.
The passage argues yields cannot rise further.
The improvement applies to every crop already.
The debate is whether the improvement will survive from laboratory to farm, and the trial evidence so far comes only from controlled Midwest conditions.
Yields will rise forty percent worldwide.
items.explanation: The passage closes by framing the debate as laboratory-to-farm transfer, with evidence limited to controlled Midwest trials. The distractors promise worldwide gains, claim unreported trials, reverse the passage's case for further gains, or extend a tobacco result to every crop.

items.question:
Is the average of a and b greater than 10?
(1) a is greater than 10.
(2) b is greater than 10.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are NOT sufficient.
items.explanation: Statement (1) alone leaves b unknown, so the average could be above or below 10, and statement (2) alone leaves a unknown. Together, a above 10 and b above 10 imply a + b is above 20, so the average is above 10. So both together are sufficient but neither alone is.

items.question:
x is a real number. Is x greater than 20?
(1) x squared minus 37x plus 342 is less than 0.
(2) x squared minus 22x plus 112 is greater than 0.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are NOT sufficient.
items.explanation: Statement (1) factors as (x - 18)(x - 19) is less than 0, so 18 < x < 19, and every value in that interval is below 20, so the answer is no and statement (1) alone is sufficient. Statement (2) factors as (x - 8)(x - 14) is greater than 0, so x is less than 8 or x is greater than 14, which leaves values on both sides of 20: x = 11 gives no and x = 25 gives yes, so it alone is not sufficient. The trap is to treat a factorised quadratic as a single bound and stop after statement (2).

items.question:
What is the value of integer n?
(1) n is a multiple of 9 between 75 and 100.
(2) n is even.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are NOT sufficient.
items.explanation: Statement (1) alone leaves 81, 90, 99 as possibilities. Statement (2) alone leaves many even numbers. Together, the only even multiple of 9 between 75 and 100 is 90, so both together are sufficient.

items.question: n is a positive integer. Is 2 to the power n minus 2 divisible by 12? (1) n is odd. (2) n is less than 5.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are NOT sufficient.
items.explanation: Step 1, the modular cycle: for n at least 2, 2 to the power n leaves remainder 4 or 8 on division by 12, so 2 to the power n minus 2 leaves remainder 2 or 6, never 0. Only n equal to 1 gives 0, which is divisible by 12. Step 2, statement (1) alone does not settle it: n equal to 1 gives yes, while n equal to 3 gives 6, not divisible by 12. Step 3, statement (2) alone does not settle it either: n equal to 1 gives yes, while n equal to 2 gives 2, not divisible by 12. Together, n is 1 or 3, so the question is still open. The answer is E.

items.question:
x and y are positive integers with x less than y. What is the value of x?
(1) x plus y equals 25.
(2) x squared plus y squared equals 325.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are NOT sufficient.
items.explanation: Statement (1) alone is not sufficient, since many pairs of positive integers with x less than y sum to 25. Statement (2) alone is not sufficient: the pairs with x squared plus y squared equals 325 are (1, 18), (6, 17) and (10, 15), so x could be 1, 6 or 10. Together, squaring the sum gives x squared plus 2xy plus y squared equals 625, so with x squared plus y squared equals 325, xy equals 150. Then x and y are the two roots of t squared minus 25t plus 150 equals 0, which are 10 and 15, and since x is less than y, x equals 10.

items.question: m and n are positive integers. Is m squared plus n squared divisible by 4? (1) m plus n is even. (2) m times n is even.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are NOT sufficient.
items.explanation: Step 1, statement (1) alone does not settle it: m equal to 1 and n equal to 1 give 2, not divisible by 4, while m equal to 2 and n equal to 2 give 8, divisible by 4. Step 2, statement (2) alone does not settle it either: m equal to 1 and n equal to 2 give 5, not divisible by 4, while m equal to 2 and n equal to 2 give 8, divisible by 4. Step 3, together: m plus n even means m and n have the same parity, and m times n even means they cannot both be odd, so both are even, and m squared plus n squared is divisible by 4. Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is. The answer is C.

items.question: Based on the table, first remove each product's highest quarterly revenue. Which product then had the largest range of quarterly revenue among its remaining three quarters, and by how much did its range exceed the second-largest range?

diagram.caption: Revenue by product and quarter, in thousands of dollars

options: (Gamma, 20 thousand dollars)
(Epsilon, 10 thousand dollars)
(Epsilon, 20 thousand dollars)
(Gamma, 10 thousand dollars)
(Epsilon, 15 thousand dollars)
items.explanation: After removing each product's best quarter, the remaining ranges are: Epsilon 55, Gamma 45, Alpha 20, Delta 20, Zeta 15, Beta 10. The largest is Epsilon at 55 and the second-largest is Gamma at 45, so the margin is 10 thousand dollars. Using the full four-quarter ranges, or a single quarter, gives the distractors.

items.question: Based on the table, first remove each product's lowest quarterly revenue. Which product then had the highest total revenue across its remaining three quarters, and by how much did its total exceed the second-highest total?
options: (Alpha, 65 thousand dollars)
(Epsilon, 55 thousand dollars)
(Alpha, 60 thousand dollars)
(Epsilon, 65 thousand dollars)
(Alpha, 55 thousand dollars)
items.explanation: After removing each product's worst quarter, the remaining totals are: Alpha 480, Epsilon 425, Delta 390, Beta 360, Gamma 355, Zeta 285. The highest is Alpha at 480 and the second-highest is Epsilon at 425, so the margin is 55 thousand dollars. Using the full four-quarter totals, or a single quarter, gives the distractors.

items.question: Which of the following statements about the table is true?
options: Zeta had the lowest median quarterly revenue.
Epsilon had the highest total annual revenue.
Gamma had the largest range of quarterly revenue.
Beta had the highest revenue in Q4.
Alpha had a lower median quarterly revenue than Zeta.
items.explanation: Check each statement against a different statistic. The lowest median belongs to Zeta (92.5 thousand dollars, from sorted quarters). The highest total is Alpha (620), not Epsilon (525). The largest range is Epsilon (65), not Gamma (50). The Q4 leader is Alpha, not Beta. And Alpha has the highest median, not a lower one than Zeta. Only the first statement is true.

items.question: Based on the chart, which group had the larger share eating the food at most infrequently, and by how many percentage points did that share exceed the other group's share eating the food at least frequently?

diagram.caption: Share of survey respondents by how often they eat the food, percent. "At most infrequently" means Infrequently, Rarely or Never; "at least occasionally" means Occasionally, Frequently or Daily; "at least frequently" means Frequently or Daily.

options: (Women, 14 points)
(Men, 6 points)
(Women, 6 points)
(Men, 14 points)
(Women, 12 points)
items.explanation: At most infrequently is Infrequently + Rarely + Never: Women 48%, Men 34%, so Women is larger. At least frequently is Daily + Frequently: Men has 42%, so the larger infrequent share exceeds it by 48 - 42 = 6 points. Using only one regrouping, or the gap within one regrouping, gives the distractors.

items.question: Based on the chart, by how many percentage points did the two groups differ in the share eating the food at least occasionally, and which group had the larger share eating the food at most infrequently?
options: (14 points, Women)
(14 points, Men)
(12 points, Women)
(12 points, Men)
(36 points, Women)
items.explanation: At least occasionally is Daily + Frequently + Occasionally: Women 52% and Men 66%, a difference of 14 points. At most infrequently is Infrequently + Rarely + Never: Women 48% and Men 34%, so Women is larger. Answering with the gap from one regrouping only, or with the wrong group, gives the distractors.

items.question: Select the pair: the group with the larger share eating the food at most infrequently, and that same group's share eating the food at least occasionally.
options: (Women, 52%)
(Women, 66%)
(Women, 30%)
items.explanation: At most infrequently is Infrequently + Rarely + Never: Women 48% and Men 34%, so Women is larger. At least occasionally is Daily + Frequently + Occasionally: Women has 52%. The pair is (Women, 52%). Using the other group's occasional share, or the frequent share instead of the occasional share, gives the distractors.

items.passage: A logistics firm operates 160 delivery vans and serves four cities. It handles 4,500 parcels a day. Its on-time delivery rate last year was 92% and its average delivery cost was $16 per parcel. The firm plans to replace diesel vans with electric vans. | Tab 2: Market Report. Industry on-time delivery averages 90%. Electric vans cost 15% more to buy but $0.20 less to run per parcel than diesel vans. Each electric charging depot costs $600 a day to run, and one depot serves the whole converted fleet. | Tab 3: Route Limits. Electric vans can only serve routes under 150 km, which carry 70% of the firm's parcels. The remaining 30% of parcels travel on long routes that diesel vans must keep serving. Customer surveys rank on-time delivery above price for urgent parcels.
items.question: Based on all three sources, which statement is best supported?

diagram.caption: Tab 1: Company Profile
diagram.content: A logistics firm operates 160 delivery vans and serves four cities. It handles 4,500 parcels a day. Its on-time delivery rate last year was 92% and its average delivery cost was $16 per parcel. The firm plans to replace diesel vans with electric vans.

options: Converting all of the firm's vans to electric would save the most money.
The depot cost means converting vans to electric can never save money.
Electric vans should be used only for the long routes.
On-time performance would fall if any vans are converted to electric.
Converting the short-route vans covers the depot cost, but converting less than about 67% of parcels would not.
items.explanation: Full conversion would save $900 a day in running costs, but only 70% of parcels are on routes electric vans can serve, so the most that can be saved is 70% of $900 = $630 a day, against a depot cost of $600 a day. The breakeven share is $600 / $900 = 66.7% of parcels, so converting less than about 67% loses money. The correct option is the statement that converting the short-route vans covers the depot cost but converting less than about 67% would not.

items.question: If the firm converts the vans serving the short routes, which carry 70% of its parcels, select the breakeven share of parcels that conversion must cover, and the expected net change in daily running cost at 70% conversion, after the depot cost.
options: (67%, a net saving of $630 a day)
(67%, a net saving of $30 a day)
(70%, a net saving of $30 a day)
(70%, a net saving of $630 a day)
(62%, a net saving of $30 a day)
items.explanation: Converting every parcel would save 4500 x $0.20 = $900 a day. The depot costs $600 a day, so conversion breaks even when it covers $600 / $900 = 67% of parcels. At 70% conversion the saving is 70% of $900 = $630 a day, less the $600 depot cost, giving a net saving of $30 a day. Forgetting the depot, or using the 70% share as the breakeven, gives the distractors.

items.passage: A retailer has 12 stores. Online sales are 38% of total sales. Average basket size online is $49 and in store is $42. The average single-channel customer spends $520 a year. | Tab 2: Customer Survey. Customers who shop both online and in store spend 25% more in total than single-channel customers. Free returns are the top reason for choosing online shopping, and each returned online order costs the retailer $4 to process. | Tab 3: Conversion Programme. Converting a single-channel customer to multi-channel shopping costs $32 a year in app support, delivery subsidies and service. The programme can target customers by their annual spend.
items.question: The programme has a budget of $48,000 a year, and converting one customer costs $32 a year, so it can convert at most 1,500 customers. Of the retailer's 2,700 single-channel customers, 1,100 spend more than $200 a year, 900 spend between $128 and $200 a year, and the rest spend less than $128 a year. Based on all three sources, which of the following statements must be true?

diagram.caption: Tab 1: Store Data
diagram.content: A retailer has 12 stores. Online sales are 38% of total sales. Average basket size online is $49 and in store is $42. The average single-channel customer spends $520 a year.

options: The average annual spend of the 1,100 customers spending more than $200 a year is at least $1,000.
The average annual spend of the 1,100 customers spending more than $200 a year is at least $1,100.
At least 550 of the 1,100 customers spending more than $200 a year each spend more than $1,031 a year.
The 1,100 customers spending more than $200 a year spend more than $1,200,000 a year in total.
The median annual spend of the 1,100 customers spending more than $200 a year is more than $1,000.
items.explanation: The average single-channel customer spends $520 a year, so the 2,700 single-channel customers spend $1,404,000 a year in total. The 900 customers between $128 and $200 a year spend at most 900 times $200, or $180,000, in total, and the 700 customers below $128 a year spend less than 700 times $128, or $89,600, in total. So the 1,100 customers above $200 a year must spend more than $1,404,000 minus $180,000 minus $89,600, which is $1,134,400, in total, an average of more than $1,031 each. Their average is therefore at least $1,000. It need not reach $1,100, the total need not reach $1,200,000, and neither a count above $1,031 nor a median above $1,000 follows, since one very high spender could carry the whole excess.

items.question: Based on the sources, what is the smallest annual spend at which converting a single-channel customer to multi-channel shopping pays for itself, and what is the net gain to the retailer from converting a customer who spends $520 a year? Select the pair (minimum spend, net gain).
items.explanation: Multi-channel customers spend 25% more, so conversion pays when 25% of annual spend exceeds the $32 conversion cost, that is above $128 a year. For a $520 customer the extra spend is 25% of $520 = $130 a year, and after the $32 conversion cost the net gain is $130 - $32 = $98 a year. Treating the conversion cost as the gain, adding it instead of subtracting it, or using the original spend as the extra gives the distractors.

items.question: Two positive integers add up to 36. Select the pair (larger number, smaller number) whose product is more than 275 and less than 321, and whose squares add up to more than 678 and less than 682.
items.explanation: Every option adds up to 36. The products are 26x10=260, 25x11=275, 22x14=308, 24x12=288, 20x16=320; the product window admits three pairs. The sums of squares are 26 squared + 10 squared = 776, 25 squared + 11 squared = 746, 22 squared + 14 squared = 680, 24 squared + 12 squared = 720, 20 squared + 16 squared = 656; only 22, 14 has its squares sum inside (678, 682). Checking only the product window, or only the sum, gives the distractors.

items.question: A rectangle has perimeter 48 cm. Select the length and width whose area is more than 108 square cm and less than 145 square cm, and whose squares of length and width add up to more than 318 and less than 322.
options: Length 18, Width 6
Length 20, Width 4
Length 12, Width 12
Length 16, Width 8
Length 17, Width 7
items.explanation: Length plus width is half the perimeter, 24 cm, which every option satisfies. The areas are 18x6=108, 20x4=80, 12x12=144, 16x8=128, 17x7=119; the area window admits three options. The sums of squares are 18 squared + 6 squared = 360, 20 squared + 4 squared = 416, 12 squared + 12 squared = 288, 16 squared + 8 squared = 320, 17 squared + 7 squared = 338; only Length 16, Width 8 has its squares sum inside (318, 322). Checking only the area window, or only the perimeter, gives the distractors.

items.question: A three-digit number has digits that add up to 18 and the number is divisible by 11. Select the greatest possible value of the number and the smallest possible value of the first digit minus the last digit.
items.explanation: Step 1, divisibility by 11: the first digit plus the last digit, minus the middle digit, must be 0 or a multiple of 11. Since the digits add to 18, the first plus the last equals 18 minus the middle digit, so that difference equals 18 minus twice the middle digit. It is 0 only when the middle digit is 9, and it is 11 or negative 11 for no integer middle digit, so the middle digit is 9 and the first plus the last digits add to 9. Step 2, the greatest number: the first digit as large as possible with the last digit as small as possible gives 990. Step 3, the smallest first-minus-last difference: the first minus the last equals twice the first digit minus 9, which is smallest when the first digit is 1, giving negative 7, at the number 189. The second option flips the sign of the difference; 981 is not divisible by 11; 189 gives the smallest difference but is not the greatest number; 900 has digits adding to 9, not 18.

items.question: A workshop has two machines. oven A alone can finish a batch of bread in 7 hours and oven B alone can finish it in 14 hours. They work on the job in turns, each working for one hour at a time, and either machine may go first. Select the shortest possible time and the longest possible time needed to finish the job.
options: (10 hours, 9.5 hours)
(9 hours, 9 hours)
(9.5 hours, 9.5 hours)
(9 hours, 10.5 hours)
(9 hours, 9.5 hours)
items.explanation: One two-hour round completes 1/7 + 1/14 = 3/14 of the job. After 4 full rounds (8 hours), 1/7 of the job remains. The fastest machine finishes the rest in the shortest time, giving 9 hours, while the slowest machine working first takes the longest, giving 9.5 hours. The correct option is (9 hours, 9.5 hours). Assuming whole hours only, or that both orders take the same time, gives the distractors.
